rationale: The four studies differ a lot in sequencing region, depth and protocol, so the pooled random forest probably spends many of its splits telling studies apart instead of finding disease signal. This change converts genus relative abundance to log scale and then standardizes each genus within each study (per-study z-score, label-free, using `ctx["meta"]["study"]` only for harmonization). That should line up the disease-related differences across studies and help the within-study AUROC.

Right now every OTU is collapsed onto its bare genus name, so all OTUs with no genus assigned (`g__`) from every family end up in one meaningless bin, and higher-level signals get lost. Those higher-level signals are the IBD hallmarks: Enterobacteriaceae up, Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae down, a Proteobacteria shift. This change builds relative-abundance features at each taxonomic level from phylum to genus, each keyed by its full lineage prefix. That should give the random forest stable signals at family and phylum level that carry across studies, and keep apart the unassigned genera that were previously merged.

Lower gut diversity is one of the most consistent IBD signals, and genus relative abundances do not capture it directly. This change adds OTU-level alpha diversity features to the existing genus random forest: Shannon, inverse Simpson, and expected richness at a fixed 1,000-read rarefaction depth, computed analytically so depth differences do not bias richness. The rest of the model is unchanged.

The case/control ratio is very different from study to study. A pooled random forest can therefore learn study-specific taxa (from sequencing region or protocol) as a stand-in for "disease", but study is constant inside each scoring group, so that shortcut adds nothing to within-study AUROC and uses up splits that could find real signal. This change reweights the training samples so cases and controls carry equal total weight inside each study, with each study keeping weight in proportion to its size. That makes study-identity taxa useless for predicting the label, so the forest has to split on disease signal that holds within studies. Study is used only to set the sample weights, never as a feature.

I'm adding a label-free prevalence filter. A genus is kept only if it is non-zero in at least 10% of the samples of at least one study. Most of the genus columns are rare, sparse genera. With `max_features="sqrt"` they take up many of the candidate splits, and the forest overfits to their noise. Requiring prevalence in at least one study, not pooled prevalence, still keeps genera that are common in one study because of its sequencing region but carry signal within that study. That fits the within-study scoring.

I'm adding the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index as features. It is the log-ratio of IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Gemellaceae) to IBD-depleted taxa (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae). I'm also adding the log abundance of each of those two groups. Being a within-sample log-ratio built on taxonomy names, the index ignores sequencing depth and is largely free of study-specific OTU and region artifacts. It packs a well-known disease signal, spread over many sparse genera, into one strong feature that transfers across studies.

I'm adding a second model and averaging the two. Alongside the unchanged study×class-weighted RF, an L2 logistic regression is trained on genus-level CLR (log-ratio) features, with each study's mean removed, and the two models' predictions are averaged by rank. The CLR model sees the many modest, roughly log-linear shifts typical of IBD dysbiosis (for example, fewer butyrate producers and more Proteobacteria), which axis-aligned splits on relative abundance pick up poorly. Removing the study mean (no labels used) cancels study-wide offsets from sequencing region and protocol. Its regularization strength is tuned by grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

The IBD hallmarks are mostly family-level shifts (Enterobacteriaceae up, Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae and Erysipelotrichaceae down). Genus assignment differs between studies because they sequenced different 16S regions, so the family level should be the steadier signal across studies. This change keeps the RF exactly as it is and gives only the per-study-centred CLR logistic regression a second block of family-level CLR features, keyed by full lineage so unassigned families stay separate. A linear model with L2 regularization tuned by inner CV can weigh the two levels against each other, which avoids the noisy extra splits that hurt the RF in round 2.

The two models are blended by ranking predictions across the whole pooled test set. Within-study AUROC is scored inside each study, though, so study-level offsets in either model (e.g. RF probabilities shifted by study-specific taxa) squeeze that model's spread inside a study and give the two models unequal weight per study. This change converts each model's scores to percentile ranks inside each test study (label-free, study used only for harmonization) before averaging, so both models count equally in every scoring group.

The CLR logistic regression currently fills zeros with a fixed 1e-5. Depth varies a lot between samples and between studies, so for shallow samples a zero becomes an extreme log value that may just mean the taxon wasn't sampled. This change records each sample's read depth in `featurize` and uses a depth-aware pseudocount (half a read, i.e. 0.5/depth) before the log-ratio step. That way zeros in shallow and deep samples sit at comparable "below detection" levels within and across studies. Nothing else changes: the RF, the weights and the rank blend stay as they are.

The random forest grows every tree to single-sample leaves. On sparse, noisy genus compositions those leaves memorise individual samples, including study-specific artefacts, and give near-binary votes, so the forest's ranking within each study comes out coarse and overfit. Requiring at least 3 samples per leaf (`min_samples_leaf=3`) averages each leaf over several samples. That should give smoother, better-calibrated scores and a better within-study AUROC; the CLR logistic regression, the weights and the rank blend are unchanged.

Lower gut diversity is one of the most consistent IBD signals. Round 3 tested diversity only inside the unweighted RF, where a few extra dense columns get diluted among the axis-aligned splits. This change computes lineage-level Shannon entropy, order-2 Rényi entropy and genus-level Shannon entropy in `featurize`. They are centred within each study (no labels used), standardized, and added only to the L2 logistic regression, which can give a smooth monotone weight to "less diverse = more likely IBD". The RF, the weights and the rank blend stay the same.

The family-level CLR block helped the logistic regression in round 8. This round adds CLR blocks at order, class and phylum level, each keyed by its full lineage and centred per study, to the L2 logistic regression only. Some IBD signals are broad shifts at those higher levels (Proteobacteria/Gammaproteobacteria up, Clostridiales/Clostridia down), and these levels should be the least affected by differences in 16S region and genus calls between studies. The RF, the weights and the rank blend are unchanged, so the noisy extra splits that hurt the RF in round 2 are avoided. The L2 penalty, tuned by inner CV, decides how much weight the new blocks get.

I'm adding a third model to the rank-average: a shallow, strongly regularised LightGBM trained on the same per-study-centred CLR and diversity features the logistic regression uses, with the same study × class weights. Boosting can pick up threshold effects and interactions in those study-harmonised log-ratios, such as a Proteobacteria bloom only together with loss of butyrate producers. Those are things the linear model can't represent, and the RF misses them because it works on raw, uncentred relative abundance. That should make the ensemble more diverse and improve the within-study ranking.

Most genus columns are rare and sparse. With `max_features="sqrt"` (about 15–20 candidates per split), many splits get no informative IBD genus to choose from, such as Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Escherichia/Shigella or Ruminococcus, so the forest splits on noise or study-specific taxa. This change gives each split a candidate pool of 25% of the genera, so splits land more often on the consistent dysbiosis markers. That should make the RF's ranking within each study more accurate; the logistic regression, the weights and the blend are unchanged.

Right now the LR features are centred within each study but scaled with one pooled SD. Studies differ in 16S region and depth, so the spread of each taxon's CLR value also differs by study, and a single coefficient means something different in each study. This change also divides each LR feature by its SD within each study (label-free; a feature that is nearly constant inside a study is set to 0 there), so coefficients act on comparable within-study units. The RF, the weights and the rank blend are unchanged.

This adds the HMP2 dysbiosis score to the logistic regression. For each sample it is the median Bray–Curtis distance (genus level and family level) to the training controls of the same study; IBD samples tend to sit far from the healthy profile of their own study. A training sample's score is computed only from controls in other grouped folds, so it never sees its own label. The scores are then centred per study and standardized like the other features. The RF, the weights and the rank blend are unchanged.

Lower richness, meaning taxa lost from the gut, is one of the most consistent IBD signals (Gevers 2014), and Shannon/Rényi entropy only partly captures it. I'm adding log expected richness at a fixed rarefaction depth of 1,000 reads to the logistic regression's per-study-centred diversity block, computed analytically at lineage, genus and family level. Depth-fixed rarefaction makes the values comparable across samples, unlike round 3, where these features went into an unweighted random forest and got diluted. The random forest, the weights and the rank blend are unchanged.

The RF and the CLR logistic regression are currently blended at a fixed 50/50, even though they probably differ in how well they rank samples within a study. This change picks the blend weight from {0.25, …, 0.75}, starting at 0.5 and moving only when the score improves by more than 0.002. The weight is chosen by within-study AUROC on out-of-fold predictions from both models, using the same grouped inner splits on the training fold that already tune the logistic regression's C.

Right now every OTU with no genus assigned (`g__`) from every family is pooled into one "g__" column. That throws away the unclassified Enterobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, which are core IBD signals, and how many OTUs lack a genus differs by study because of sequencing region. This change sends each unassigned OTU to "unclassified <deepest assigned lineage>" in the shared genus block that feeds both the RF and the CLR logistic regression. It adds only a few dozen columns, unlike round 2, which put every taxonomic level into an unweighted RF; everything else stays the same.
